items.question: What is the primary purpose of fixed floats on the R44 II, and what does the supplement say about intentional water landings?
options: Use them for frequent, planned water landings instead of runways
Use them as a safety feature when flying over water; avoid intentional water landings for purposes other than training
Use them only as decoration; they provide no real safety benefit
Use them only for planned water ditchings
items.explanation: The Fixed Floats supplement states that the float landing gear is intended as a safety feature for flights over water, and that intentional (non-emergency) water landings for purposes other than training are not recommended.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: FIXED FLOATS SUPPLEMENT (p.9-5.2)

items.question: With fixed floats installed, what is Vne at takeoff gross weight above 2200 lb according to the supplement?
options: 100 KIAS
110 KIAS
120 KIAS
130 KIAS
items.explanation: The Fixed Floats supplement specifies Vne 110 KIAS at TOGW above 2200 lb, 120 KIAS at 2200 lb and below, and 100 KIAS in autorotation.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: FIXED FLOATS SUPPLEMENT (p.9-5.2)

items.question: How does the Pop-Out Floats supplement describe certification for ditching and recommended use?
options: Pop-out floats are certified for ditching and recommended for planned water landings
Pop-out floats are not certified for ditching; use them as a safety feature when flying over water, not for intentional water landings
Pop-out floats are only decorative and must not be used for water landings
Pop-out floats are approved for land operations only
items.explanation: The Pop-Out Floats supplement states that the pop-out floats are intended as a safety feature for flight over water, that intentional water landings for purposes other than training are not recommended, and that the system is not certified for ditching.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: POP-OUT FLOATS SUPPLEMENT (p.9-10.2)

items.question: When the pop-out floats are inflated, what maximum IAS must you not exceed?
options: 70 KIAS
80 KIAS
100 KIAS
115 KIAS
items.explanation: The airspeed limitations in the Pop-Out Floats supplement state that 80 KIAS is the maximum airspeed both for inflation and with the floats inflated.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: POP-OUT FLOATS SUPPLEMENT (p.9-10.3)

items.question: What altitude restriction applies to inflation of the pop-out floats according to the supplement?
options: Inflate the floats at any altitude as long as IAS is below 80 KIAS
Do not inflate the floats above 2000 ft AGL
Do not inflate the floats above 4000 ft AGL, and limit altitude loss with inflated floats to 4000 ft
Always inflate the floats on the ground before takeoff
items.explanation: The Pop-Out Floats supplement states that the maximum altitude loss with inflated floats is 4000 ft and warns against inflating the floats above 4000 ft AGL to avoid loss of shape and stiffness.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: POP-OUT FLOATS SUPPLEMENT (p.9-10.3)

items.question: Which maneuver is specifically warned against in autorotation or water landing with floats because it can cause the helicopter to nose over?
options: Flaring aggressively with aft cyclic at 10–15 ft AGL
Closing the mixture before you have flared
Lowering collective rapidly or using large forward cyclic while the helicopter still has forward speed on the water
Holding collective fully up until after the helicopter has stopped
items.explanation: Both the Fixed Floats and Pop-Out Floats supplements include a CAUTION warning that rapid collective reduction or large forward cyclic while the helicopter is moving forward on the water can cause the floats to dig in and the helicopter to nose over.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: FIXED FLOATS & POP-OUT FLOATS SUPPLEMENTS (p.9-5.3, p.9-10.4)

items.question: When is it recommended to use pitot heat according to the Heated Pitot supplement, and what is emphasized about flight in icing?
options: Keep pitot heat on all the time in flight; the helicopter is approved for flight in known icing
Use pitot heat only during takeoff and landing; flight in icing is allowed as long as IAS is above 70 KIAS

Turn pitot heat on whenever conditions are conducive to pitot icing and leave it on until landing or until you are out of potential icing conditions; the helicopter is still not certified for flight in known or suspected icing
Use pitot heat only during maintenance checks
items.explanation: The Heated Pitot supplement says that pitot heat should be used when conditions are conducive to pitot icing, but a NOTE emphasizes that the R44 is not certified for flight in known or suspected icing.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: HEATED PITOT SUPPLEMENT (p.9-6.2)

items.question: What is an important consequence of leaving pitot heat on after an engine or alternator failure, according to the supplement?
options: It has no effect as long as rotor RPM remains within limits
It will reduce rotor RPM because the heater takes torque from the engine
It will significantly increase battery drain and can discharge the battery more quickly
It will automatically shed other non-essential electrical loads
items.explanation: The Heated Pitot supplement has a NOTE stating that continued use of pitot heat after an engine or alternator failure will significantly increase battery drain.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: HEATED PITOT SUPPLEMENT (p.9-6.2)

items.question: How is the air conditioning system controlled, and what is normally observed on the ground according to the Air Conditioning supplement?
options: Use a rotary thermostat on the panel; fluid leaking under the helicopter indicates a malfunction
Use a toggle switch with OFF/LOW/HIGH on the forward end of the overhead duct; condensate draining through a belly tube and dripping on the ground is normal
The system is controlled automatically by OAT and requires no pilot action; water should never drip from the helicopter
The system is controlled only via a menu in the GPS
items.explanation: The Air Conditioning supplement describes a switch with OFF, LOW and HIGH on the forward end of the overhead duct; the compressor engages automatically when the fan is turned on, and a NOTE explains that condensate drains through a belly tube and that water on the ground under the helicopter during operation is normal.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: AIR CONDITIONING SUPPLEMENT (p.9-11.2)

items.question: What does the Police Version supplement say about removing the nose camera, and what must the pilot do before flying without the camera?
options: No special effect; no additional calculations are required
It causes a large CG shift; perform a new weight and balance calculation to ensure the aft CG limit is not exceeded
The helicopter becomes too nose-heavy and cannot be flown without the camera
Only seats and baggage need adjustment, not weight and balance
items.explanation: In the weight and balance section of the Police Version supplement there is a CAUTION stating that removal of the nose camera causes a large change in empty weight CG, and that weight and balance must be calculated before flight to ensure the aft CG limit is not exceeded.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: POLICE VERSION SUPPLEMENT (p.9-7.3)

items.question: What does it mean that the HeliSAS autopilot is a 'fly through' system, according to the supplement?
options: The pilot must completely release the cyclic for the autopilot to work
The autopilot controls collective and pedals but not cyclic
The autopilot always disconnects with any manual cyclic movement
The pilot can override the autopilot with a few pounds of stick force without disconnecting it, and the autopilot provides no input to collective or pedals
items.explanation: The HeliSAS supplement explains that the system provides corrective input only to the cyclic, not to the collective or pedals, and that it is a 'fly through' system where the pilot can override with a few pounds of stick force without disconnecting the autopilot.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: HELISAS AUTOPILOT SUPPLEMENT (p.9-13.2)

items.question: What is the minimum height AGL for using the autopilot ALT mode according to the HeliSAS supplement?
options: 50 ft AGL
200 ft AGL
500 ft AGL
1000 ft AGL
items.explanation: In the LIMITATIONS section of the HeliSAS supplement it states that the minimum height for use of ALT mode is 200 ft AGL.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: HELISAS AUTOPILOT SUPPLEMENT (p.9-13.3)

items.question: What does the Optional Avionics supplement recommend regarding the use of traditional flight instruments versus PFD/MFD?
options: Always use the PFD/MFD as primary instruments and ignore the traditional instruments
Remove traditional instruments when a PFD is installed
Keep traditional instruments and use them as primary instruments unless you are fully familiar with the installed avionics
Use the PFD/MFD only when an instructor is present
items.explanation: The Optional Avionics supplement states that with Robinson PFD/MFD installations the traditional instruments are retained, and that pilots should use these as primary instruments unless they are fully familiar with the installed avionics.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: OPTIONAL AVIONICS SUPPLEMENT (p.9-14.2)

items.question: What is the main point of the CAUTION text in the Garmin GPSMAP 225 supplement related to night flight?
options: The dimmer will always be too weak for night flying; do not use the unit in darkness
The dimmer may be insufficient for night flying; if necessary you can further reduce brightness by increasing the contrast setting via the AUX/System Setup menu
The screen adjusts brightness automatically and should not be changed manually
The unit is approved only for day VFR
items.explanation: The GPSMAP 225 supplement contains a CAUTION noting that the dimmer does not always dim enough for night flying, and recommends that if necessary the pilot further reduce brightness by adjusting contrast via the Auxiliary/System Setup menus according to the pilot's guide.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: GARMIN GPSMAP 225 SUPPLEMENT (p.9-9.2)

items.question: What does the BATT FAULT warning mean in the Lithium-Ion Battery supplement, and what should the pilot do?
options: It is only a test light; continue the flight
It indicates abnormal battery operation (such as over/undervoltage, overtemperature or excessive current draw); land as soon as practical, but the alternator will continue to supply power in flight
It means both battery and alternator have failed; immediately shed all electrical load
It only means the battery heater is active
items.explanation: The Lithium-Ion Battery supplement explains that the BATT FAULT light indicates abnormal battery operation and that charging and/or discharging functions may be disabled. The procedure is to land as soon as practical; the alternator will continue to provide power in flight.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: LITHIUM-ION BATTERY SUPPLEMENT (p.9-15.2)

items.question: What pressure limits apply to fixed floats, and how should you plan around them before landing when you expect changes in altitude and temperature?
options: Keep pressure between 0.5 and 2.0 psig regardless of flight profile
Keep pressure between 1.5 and 5.0 psig and plan inflation so there is still at least 1.5 psig at landing
Always pump to maximum pressure; the relief valves will vent as needed in normal use
Rely on the system to self-regulate; there are no numerical limits
items.explanation: The Fixed Floats supplement specifies a minimum float pressure of 1.5 psig and a maximum of 5 psig, and explains how to account for expected decreases in altitude/temperature so that pressure at landing is still at least 1.5 psig.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: FIXED FLOATS SUPPLEMENT (p.9-5.4)

items.question: What is the main point of the warnings about adverse roll and sideslip with inflated fixed floats?
options: Use a lot of sideslip to improve visibility during water landing
Keep the helicopter trimmed with zero sideslip; sideslip can produce opposite roll and loss of control, especially during simulated engine failures
Use only right pedal; left pedal is prohibited with floats
Apply high cyclic friction to dampen movements in turbulence
items.explanation: In the NORMAL PROCEDURES and Safety Tips sections for fixed floats it is emphasized that the helicopter has unfavorable roll characteristics with floats inflated, and that sideslip can produce roll in the opposite direction and potentially loss of control. Therefore the helicopter should be kept trimmed with near zero sideslip, especially during simulated engine failures.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: FIXED FLOATS SUPPLEMENT (p.9-5.7, p.9-5.13)

items.question: What do the supplements describe as typical limitations for wave height and water taxi operations with floats?
options: Safe operation in waves up to 3 ft and no limitation on taxi speed
Safe operation in waves up to about 1 ft and a recommended maximum water taxi speed around 5 knots
Only glassy-smooth water is allowed, but taxi speed may be up to 20 knots
Only fresh water is permitted; sea water is explicitly prohibited
items.explanation: Both the Fixed Floats and Pop-Out Floats supplements state that safe operation has been demonstrated in waves up to about 1 ft (0.3 m) and recommend a maximum water taxi speed of around 5 knots with some collective applied.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: FIXED FLOATS SUPPLEMENT (p.9-5.8)
R44 II POH Sec 9: POP-OUT FLOATS SUPPLEMENT (p.9-10.9)

items.question: How should the safety catch on the inflation lever for pop-out floats be set for over-water flight versus flight over land, and what speed limit follows from the READY position?
options: Always leave the safety catch in READY; it does not impose any additional speed limit
Set the safety catch to READY before over-water flight and back to LOCKED over land; with the safety catch in READY Vne is 115 KIAS even with the floats stowed
Always leave the safety catch in LOCKED in all flight; READY is only used during maintenance
Use READY only during landing and takeoff; otherwise its position is irrelevant
items.explanation: The Pop-Out Floats supplement states that the safety catch must be in the READY position before flight over water so that the floats can be inflated, and back to LOCKED over land. When the safety catch is in READY there is a specific Vne limit of 115 KIAS even when the floats are still stowed.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: POP-OUT FLOATS SUPPLEMENT (p.9-10.3, p.9-10.7)

items.question: According to the Pop-Out Floats supplement, how long can inflation take after you pull the red inflation lever, and what does this imply for when you must activate it before a water landing?
options: The floats inflate immediately; activate the lever as late as possible to avoid drag
The floats may take up to about three seconds to inflate; squeeze the inflation lever early enough that the floats are full before water contact
The floats need at least ten seconds to inflate; activate the lever as soon as you see water on the horizon
Inflation time varies so much that the supplement recommends ignoring the timing
items.explanation: In the EMERGENCY PROCEDURES section for pop-out floats it states that inflation can take up to about three seconds, and a CAUTION instructs the pilot to squeeze the inflation lever early enough that the floats are fully inflated before contacting the water.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: POP-OUT FLOATS SUPPLEMENT (p.9-10.4)

items.question: What is the purpose of the safety pin on the pressure cylinder in the pop-out float system, and what is operationally critical to remember?
options: It locks the helicopter on the ground; fly with the pin installed for extra safety
It prevents unintentional pressure release during maintenance and transport and must be removed for all normal flight; with the pin installed you cannot inflate the floats from the cockpit
It is an emergency release to dump float pressure during a water landing
It is used only to measure cylinder pressure during the daily inspection
items.explanation: The supplement explains that the safety pin at the valve on the pressure cylinder is intended for maintenance and transport, and that it must not be installed during normal operation. With the pin installed, the inflation lever in the cockpit cannot inflate the floats.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: POP-OUT FLOATS SUPPLEMENT (p.9-10.8, p.9-10.13)

items.question: How does the Police Version supplement describe seat configuration and baggage options when police equipment is installed?
options: The helicopter remains a four-seater; all seats and baggage compartments may be used normally
The helicopter becomes a three-seater; the right rear seat is replaced by a cover that cannot be occupied, and baggage is not permitted in the right rear baggage compartment
Only the two front seats may be used; no baggage is allowed
All seats may be used, but baggage is only permitted in the right rear baggage compartment
items.explanation: The Police Version supplement states that the R44 becomes a three-seat helicopter when police equipment is installed, that the right rear seat is replaced by a cover that cannot be occupied, and that baggage is not permitted in the right rear baggage compartment because of electronics and cabling located there.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: POLICE VERSION SUPPLEMENT (p.9-7.2, p.9-7.3)

items.question: What does the Police Version supplement say about handling and risks associated with the belly-mounted searchlight?
options: Keep the searchlight pointed straight down at all times; no special hazards are mentioned
Stow the searchlight horizontally when not in use to reduce the risk of damage in a hard landing, and be aware that both its brightness and heat can disorient others and cause burns at close range
Keep the searchlight on maximum intensity to better see your own position
Avoid using it at night; the supplement prohibits night use of the searchlight
items.explanation: In the SYSTEMS DESCRIPTION section the belly-mounted searchlight is described, and it is emphasized that it should be stowed horizontally when not in use to reduce damage in a hard landing. The supplement also warns that the searchlight is very bright and hot and can disorient or burn others at close range.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: POLICE VERSION SUPPLEMENT (p.9-7.3, p.9-7.6)

items.question: What weight limitation and NO STOWAGE placards are described in the ENG Version supplement?
options: Maximum 200 lb in the left front seat; no special placards
Maximum 250 lb (113 kg) in the left front seat; NO STOWAGE placards under the left front seat and in the right rear equipment bay
Maximum 300 lb in the left front seat; NO STOWAGE only in the left rear corner
No specific weight limits; only a requirement for cargo nets
items.explanation: The ENG Version supplement specifies a maximum weight of 250 lb (113 kg) in the left front seat and describes NO STOWAGE placards under the left front seat and in the right rear equipment bay where ENG equipment is installed.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: E.N.G. VERSION SUPPLEMENT (p.9-8.2)

items.question: According to the emergency procedures in the ENG Version supplement, what should you do with the ENG equipment in the event of an engine failure above 500 ft AGL?
options: Leave all ENG equipment extended; focus only on the autorotation
Stow the laptop controller and video titler keyboard and retract the omni antenna if time permits
Disconnect the battery before starting the autorotation
Turn on the searchlight and camera to document the event
items.explanation: In the EMERGENCY PROCEDURES for the ENG version it states that in the event of a power loss above 500 ft AGL the laptop controller and video titler keyboard should be stowed and the omni antenna retracted if time permits, before carrying out the autorotation.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: E.N.G. VERSION SUPPLEMENT (p.9-8.3)

items.question: What is the main point of the CAUTION text about the laptop controller in the ENG Version supplement?
options: It is very sensitive to cold and must always be kept warm
It is heavy and can injure people in a hard landing if not properly secured; it must always be secured during taxi, takeoff, and landing
It cannot tolerate water and must be removed before flight over water
It must never be used during stabilized flight
items.explanation: The Systems Description for the ENG version states that the laptop controller is heavy and can cause injury in a hard landing if not properly secured, and the CAUTION text requires that it be secured during taxi, takeoff, and landing.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: E.N.G. VERSION SUPPLEMENT (p.9-8.5)

items.question: What does the HeliSAS supplement specify about keeping a hand on the cyclic and the minimum altitudes for ALT and VRT modes?
options: The pilot may release the cyclic completely when the autopilot is on; ALT and VRT may be used all the way down to the surface

The pilot must keep a hand on the cyclic during autopilot engagement and disengagement and below 200 ft AGL; the minimum altitude for ALT mode is 200 ft AGL, and for VRT mode during practice approaches it is 50 ft AGL
The pilot must always fly with two hands on the cyclic; ALT and VRT may only be used above 1000 ft AGL
There are no specific requirements for hand on cyclic or altitude in the supplement
items.explanation: In the LIMITATIONS section for HeliSAS it states that the pilot's hand must be on the cyclic grip during engagement and disengagement and at altitudes below 200 ft AGL. The minimum altitude for ALT mode is 200 ft AGL, and during practice ILS/GPS approaches the minimum altitude for VRT mode is 50 ft AGL.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: HELISAS AUTOPILOT SUPPLEMENT (p.9-13.3)

items.question: What does the HeliSAS supplement say about the use of cyclic friction when the autopilot is engaged?
options: Increase cyclic friction to help the autopilot hold heading
Use moderate friction only in turbulence; otherwise it is optional
Keep cyclic friction fully off; friction degrades autopilot performance
It does not matter; friction only affects manual flying
items.explanation: Under NORMAL PROCEDURES it explicitly states that cyclic friction must be fully off for the autopilot to work properly, and that friction will degrade autopilot performance.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: HELISAS AUTOPILOT SUPPLEMENT (p.9-13.4)

items.question: How is responsibility for altitude and airspeed divided between the HeliSAS autopilot and the pilot in ALT and VRT modes?
options: The autopilot controls both cyclic and collective and independently maintains airspeed and rate of climb/descent
The autopilot provides only pedal input; the pilot controls everything else
The autopilot uses pitch via the cyclic to hold altitude or follow the glidepath but has no control over power; the pilot must control collective and power with small, smooth changes
ALT and VRT modes are only visual cues and do not affect the controls
items.explanation: The HeliSAS supplement explains in the description of ALT and VRT modes that the autopilot uses pitch via the cyclic to hold altitude or follow the glidepath, but does not control power. The pilot must control collective and power with small, smooth changes to manage airspeed and rate of climb or descent.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: HELISAS AUTOPILOT SUPPLEMENT (p.9-13.9)

items.question: What does the HeliSAS supplement say about using the autopilot in IMC (instrument meteorological conditions)?
options: The autopilot is approved for IFR/IMC and may be used as the primary means of control
The autopilot may be used in light IMC as long as SAS mode is active
The autopilot is not certified for flight in IMC; you must still remain within VFR minima and use the autopilot only as workload relief
There is no mention of IMC in the supplement
items.explanation: In the SAFETY TIPS section it is emphasized that the autopilot is not certified for use in instrument conditions (IMC) and that it remains essential to operate within applicable VFR weather minima and use the autopilot as an aid, not as a replacement for the pilot's responsibility.
references: R44 II POH Sec 9: HELISAS AUTOPILOT SUPPLEMENT (p.9-13.13)
